# AGENTS.md

Instructions for AI coding agents working on this repository. People: the
same rules apply to you.

## Read this first

**Cross-Store Owned** is a Firefox extension, generated by AI under human
direction. What it does: badges games on Steam that you already own on GOG, and games on GOG that you already own on Steam.

The maintainer does not read code. A change is judged by two things only:

1. **The automated checks.** They run on every pull request. A pull request
   that fails them is not merged.
2. **Trying it.** Before merging, the maintainer tries the change in real
   Firefox, using the steps you write in the pull request.

So your job is a change that passes the checks, explained so that someone who
won't read the code can try it.

## What's where

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `manifest.json` | The extension's main settings file. Firefox loads this folder as-is |
| `background.js`, `content/`, `lib/`, `popup/`, `options/`, `icons/` | The extension itself |
| `docs/spec.md` | What the extension should do. **Read it before changing behaviour** |
| `docs/` | How it works (`architecture.md`), setting up and debugging (`development.md`), research on the stores' pages and services (`learnings.md`) |
| `tests/` | The automated tests, and the hand-made test pages they run against |
| `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` | For users |

**Shipped** files are the ones that go into the signed extension people
install. Everything is shipped except `README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/`,
`tests/` and the repository's own files (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
`UNLICENSE`, `.github/`, `.claude/`, `.gitignore`).

## Checking your work

You need Node.js 22.22 or newer. Once, put the shared tools next to this
repository:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/inklikeurine/firefox-tools ../firefox-tools
npm install --prefix ../firefox-tools
npx --prefix ../firefox-tools playwright install firefox
```

Then, from this repository's folder:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `node ../firefox-tools/tools/check.mjs cross-store-owned` | **Validate**: file layout, `manifest.json`, README sections, every `.js` file parses, no undefined or unused names, no forbidden code, and `web-ext lint` (Mozilla's own checker) |
| `node ../firefox-tools/harness/run.mjs cross-store-owned --tests` | **Tests**: the suites in `tests/`, run without a browser. Fast; run these often |
| `node ../firefox-tools/harness/run.mjs cross-store-owned --spec` | **Tests and live check**: the tests, then installs the extension into a hidden Firefox, opens the test pages and runs the checks in `tests/harness.json` |

The pull request checks run exactly these. Run them before you push and fix
anything that fails. Never weaken a check or a test to get it to pass.

Every pull request also runs **guards** for the rules marked below: no
editing existing tests, no new permissions or web addresses, no changes to
the files that control the checks. They run from the maintainer's copy of the
checks, so a pull request can't switch them off. When one fails, it says
which rule and what to do.

## Writing code

These keep the extension safe and able to pass Mozilla's review:

- **Plain JavaScript, no build step.** No `package.json`, bundler,
  transpiler or `node_modules` in this repository. The folder must load
  in Firefox exactly as it is.
- **Firefox 140 or newer, on desktop.** Nothing for Chrome, Edge, Safari or
  Firefox for Android.
- **No `eval`, `new Function`, remote scripts or inline `<script>`.** Mozilla
  rejects them.
- **No `innerHTML` except with fixed text.** Build elements with
  `createElement` and `textContent`.
- **Ask for as little as possible.** Add a permission only when the feature
  can't work without it, and explain it in the README's Permissions table.
- **New permissions and new websites need the maintainer's OK.** The checks
  fail if a pull request adds anything to `permissions`,
  `optional_permissions`, `host_permissions`, `content_security_policy` or a
  content script's `matches` in `manifest.json`, or adds a web address
  (`http://` or `https://`) that the shipped code didn't contain before.
  Explain in the pull request what it's for. Only the maintainer can allow
  it, by adding the `new-access` label.
- **Each store's selectors stay at the top of its adapter**
  (`content/steam.js`, `content/gog.js`), not spread through the code, so a
  store change is a one-file fix. Prefer `id`, `aria-*` and `data-*`
  attributes over class names that look machine-generated.
- **Look it up, don't go from memory.** Firefox's extension APIs change.
  Before using a `browser.*` API or a `manifest.json` key, read its current
  page on MDN (developer.mozilla.org).
- **Fail quietly.** A missing element, a page that refuses the extension, or
  broken stored settings: log one warning and keep the rest working. Startup
  never throws an error.
- **Content scripts can run twice** on the same page (reloads, page changes).
  The second run must not attach anything twice.
- **Nothing leaves the browser** unless the feature needs it, and the README
  says so.
- Log with `console.warn` or `console.error`, starting with `[cross-store-owned]`.
  No `console.log` in shipped code.

Rules for this extension:

- **It talks to Steam, GOG and IsThereAnyDeal**, and nothing else
  (`docs/architecture.md`). Any other web address needs the maintainer's OK
  (see above).

Don't change:

- the extension ID, `cross-store-owned@inklikeurine.dev`. Firefox recognises the installed extension by
  it, so changing it breaks every existing install
- `strict_min_version` (`140.0`)
- the license: the Unlicense only, and no license or copyright lines at the
  top of files

## Tests

A test is only worth something if it can't be faked, so the pull request
checks guard the tests themselves:

- **Add tests; don't change existing ones.** A pull request may add new
  tests, new test pages and new entries in `tests/harness.json`. The checks
  fail if any existing line in `tests/` is removed or changed. If an existing
  test really is wrong (for example, a website changed), explain why in the
  pull request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `tests-changed` label. When behaviour changes on purpose, don't leave the
  old test standing beside a new one: say in the pull request which existing
  tests are now wrong, so they can be changed with the label or removed in
  the next test tidy-up.
- **Your new tests must fail without your change.** The checks run your
  pull request's tests against the code on `main` and list each new or
  changed test. If none of them fail there, they aren't testing your change,
  and the check fails. Any that pass there too are named: say in the pull
  request why each is needed, or leave it out. A change to
  shipped code needs at least one such test. If a change really can't have
  one (a clean-up that changes no behaviour, say), explain why in the pull
  request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the `no-test-needed`
  label.
- **A test checks what it is about.** Check the entries, values or keys the
  test is about, not a whole list around them, so that adding a setting or a
  button breaks only the tests about it. One test may pin a whole list on
  purpose (every setting, in order); mark it with a `// the whole list`
  comment. The validator warns about any other.
- **The tests get tidied.** Since a pull request can only add tests, the
  maintainer asks now and then (with a release, say) for a test tidy-up: a
  pull request that removes tests that are repeated, cover behaviour that is
  gone, or test nothing, and says in plain words what each one was and which
  test still covers it. It changes no shipped code, and needs the
  `tests-changed` label.
- **Test pages copy the shape of the real pages.** The pages in
  `tests/fixtures/` are hand-made: the same elements and attributes as the
  real page, filled with made-up data only. No real names, emails or account
  details, and never a saved copy of a signed-in page. The maintainer
  compares new or changed test pages against the real pages before merging.

Passing tests don't prove a change is right; they prove it didn't break what
was already checked. The maintainer trying it in Firefox is still the last
word.

## Documentation

- If behaviour, permissions or settings change, update `README.md` and the
  matching file in `docs/` in the same pull request.
- The README and `docs/` describe the extension **as it is now**. No "used
  to…" or "fixed in 0.3". History lives in `CHANGELOG.md` only.

## Versions and the changelog: leave them alone

**Don't change `version` in `manifest.json`, and don't edit `CHANGELOG.md`.**
The maintainer does both, once, in a release pull request when a batch of
changes is ready to ship. Mozilla signs each version number only once, so a
version number is only used up by a real release.

## Your pull request

Fill in the pull request template. Most importantly:

- **One fix or feature per pull request.**
- **Say which AI tool wrote it**, and roughly how much of it.
- **Report three checks by these exact names**, and tick only what was
  actually done:
  - **Validated**: `check.mjs` passed.
  - **Automated Test**: `run.mjs --spec` passed (tests and live check).
  - **Manual Review**: leave unticked. It means a person tried the change in
    real Firefox, and the maintainer does that before merging.
- **Write "How to try it"** as numbered steps. Each step is something to do
  and what should happen, for example "Open a Steam store page for a game
  you own on GOG. A badge appears on it." "Check that it works" is not a
  step. Write the steps from your change, not the whole extension: a
  one-line fix gets one or two steps.

**Never say a change was "tested in Firefox" or "works" unless a person
tried it in real Firefox.** Passing the checks is not the same thing. Say
exactly what you ran.

## Don't

- Don't commit personal data: names, emails, addresses, screenshots of a
  signed-in website, or details of your own computer or network.
- **Don't change the files that control the checks or the maintainer's AI
  tools:** `.github/`, `.claude/`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. The checks
  fail if a pull request touches them. If a change is really needed, explain
  why in the pull request. Only the maintainer can allow it, by adding the
  `rules-changed` label.
- Don't create or delete tags or releases, or delete branches other than
  your own.
